subtype: Scheduling time to open the box [Response]
passage:
At the milk collection centre outside Moga, the morning line of farmers never stopped, and Baljeet had no room for the letter from the cooperative board about falling fat readings. Each time the worry rose, he wrote one word on a scrap of paper, "board", "machine", "Yogesh?", and pushed it into his shirt pocket.
At six, after the last can was weighed, he walked to the tube-well and sat on its concrete edge with the scraps and a cup of tea. For twenty minutes the worry got its turn: the tight chest, the fear of losing the contract, the question of whether the testing machine was faulty. Then one plan: ask Yogesh, the mechanic, to check the machine tomorrow. The scraps went back in the pocket, and Baljeet went home for dinner.

qa.q: What did Baljeet write on the scraps of paper?
qa.a: One word each time the worry rose, such as "board", "machine" and "Yogesh?".

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel during the twenty minutes at the tube-well?
qa.a: A tight chest and fear of losing the contract; he let that anxiety be felt fully in the time he had set aside for it.

qa.q: Why does the scrap-and-tube-well routine work?
qa.a: It lets him set worries aside during the busy line but gives them a door: a fixed time to feel them and make one plan, like asking Yogesh to check the machine.

qa.q: How might the farmers in the morning line experience Baljeet?
qa.a: They probably see a focused, steady person weighing their milk, without knowing about the worry in his pocket.

grounding: A young adult sets aside a work worry during the busy day and deliberately gives it a fixed evening time to be felt and acted on.

subtype: Hiding behind a parent at a party [Actor]
passage:
Note to Anjali's mother, after the Diwali mela at school.
Anjali held your leg for the first half hour and hid her face whenever anyone said hello. When Irawati from her class waved, she buried herself deeper. I didn't ask her to greet anyone. I just sat on the mat near you and started making a paper lantern. After a while she peeped out, then crept closer, then held the glue for me. She never said hello, but she stayed by the lanterns till the end.
Next week I will keep the lantern corner open at playtime.

qa.q: What did the note-writer start making on the mat?
qa.a: A paper lantern.

qa.q: Why did Anjali hide her face when people said hello?
qa.a: She felt shy and frightened by all the greetings 🥺, and hiding behind her mother's leg brought relief.

qa.q: What helped Anjali come out, and what comes next?
qa.a: Sitting nearby without pushing and doing a calm activity let her come closer at her own pace; keeping the lantern corner open at playtime continues that.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel when Anjali hides from her wave?
qa.a: Irawati may feel puzzled or a little disappointed, not knowing Anjali was scared rather than unfriendly.

grounding: A young child clings to her mother and will not greet anyone at a school mela, and gentle nearness helps her come closer.

subtype: Not looking at the difficult homework [Actor]
passage:
It was Bonfire Night in Leeds, and the fractions sheet had been on Daniel's desk since tea. He sharpened three pencils. He lined up his rubbers by size. He went down for water, then again because the first glass was "too warm". From the window he could see rockets bursting over the park.
"Done yet?" called Siddiq, the older boy from next door who helped him with homework.
"Nearly," Daniel said. He hadn't written a single number. Every time he looked at question one, his tummy went tight, and tidying made the tight feeling go away.
By eight his desk was spotless and the sheet was blank. Next week, he thought, he would tidy the drawers first.

qa.q: How many pencils did Daniel sharpen?
qa.a: Three pencils.

qa.q: Why did Daniel keep tidying instead of starting question one?
qa.a: Looking at the fractions made his tummy tight with worry, and tidying brought quick relief, so escaping felt good.

qa.q: What small step would help Daniel?
qa.a: Ask Siddiq to sit with him for just question one, or set a timer for five minutes of trying 🙂, so he learns the tight feeling passes.

qa.q: What might Siddiq think when Daniel says "Nearly"?
qa.a: Siddiq probably believes him or hopes it is true, and may be surprised later to find the sheet blank.

grounding: A child avoids hard homework by tidying and fetching water, and the relief makes him plan to escape again.

passage:
Counsellor's note, first week after the summer holidays.
Yogesh came in on Tuesday asking about "something unrelated". Twenty minutes in, he showed me his phone. A message from his friend Gurpreet, sent eleven days ago during the holidays, was still unread; the preview began, "I'm really upset about what you said at the". He told me he had seen the preview, felt his stomach drop, and kept meaning to answer "when I know what to say". Each day it got harder. Now Gurpreet sits at a different desk, and Yogesh feels, in his words, "like the worst person alive".
We opened the message together. It was shorter than he feared. He drafted a two-line reply: sorry for going silent, can we talk at lunch? I will check in with him on Friday.

qa.q: How long ago had Gurpreet sent the message?
qa.a: Eleven days ago, during the holidays.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh leave the message unopened for so long?
qa.a: He felt a drop of dread and guilt, and waiting until he knew what to say felt easier than facing it, though each day made it heavier.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped?
qa.a: Opened the message with him, which showed it was shorter than feared, helped him draft a simple two-line reply, and planned a Friday check-in.

qa.q: What might those eleven days have been like for Gurpreet?
qa.a: Gurpreet was already upset and then heard nothing, likely feeling ignored and hurt enough to move to a different desk.

grounding: A teenager leaves a friend's upset message unread for days, and the delay makes the guilt and the conversation bigger.

subtype: Dodging a hard talk with a friend [Actor]
passage:
Before: On the first night of Navratri, Jeevan laughed at Aadhya's garba steps in front of the whole hostel group. "Did you learn from a video with no sound?" Everyone laughed. Aadhya smiled and felt her face burn.
During: Four days later, when the group chat planned the big garba night, Aadhya replied, "can't, assignment 😅", and stayed in her room hearing the music through the window. She hoped the sting would just fade.
After: By Dussehra the chat had a new inside joke she didn't understand. Jeevan messaged: "Haven't seen you all week. Did I do something?" Aadhya typed "no, all good!" and put the phone face down. The relief lasted a minute. The distance stayed.

qa.q: What did Aadhya reply when the group planned garba night?
qa.a: "can't, assignment".

qa.q: Why did Aadhya tell Jeevan "no, all good!"?
qa.a: She still felt hurt by the joke, but talking about it felt harder than hiding, so brushing it off brought a minute of relief.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try instead?
qa.a: Answer Jeevan's opening honestly, for example "The joke about my steps stung", giving the friendship a chance to be repaired.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel about Aadhya's distance?
qa.a: Jeevan seems confused and a little worried, asking "Did I do something?" without knowing the joke hurt.

grounding: A young adult hurt by a friend's joke goes quiet and skips plans, and the short relief costs the friendship a chance at repair.

passage:
Before: Ayesha had always been the loudest in the back row, but the Monday after results came out, her seat was empty. Pallavi saw "Fluid Mechanics: F" on the list and texted her. No reply.
During: On Thursday Pallavi found her at the canteen. When Pallavi mentioned the supplementary exam, Ayesha laughed too fast. "Let's not. Tell me about your cousin's wedding instead." She left before her chai had cooled.
After: The next Monday Pallavi didn't lecture. She sat down with two samosas and said, "I'm going to the library at four anyway. Want to come just to look at the syllabus? Ten minutes, then we leave."
Ayesha stared at the samosa for a while. "Only ten minutes," she said. At four, she was there.

qa.q: What grade did Ayesha get in Fluid Mechanics?
qa.a: An F.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Ayesha laughed too fast and left?
qa.a: Pallavi felt worried and a little helpless, seeing her lively friend dodge the topic and pull away.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi's offer work where mentioning the exam did not?
qa.a: It gave company and a tiny, concrete first step, just ten minutes with the syllabus, instead of pressure or a lecture.

qa.q: What might the failed subject feel like for Ayesha?
qa.a: Probably embarrassing and frightening, so avoiding classes and conversations felt safer than facing it.

grounding: A friend notices a lively student avoiding classes after failing a subject and offers company and a small first step.

subtype: Approaching the fear in small steps [Response]
passage:
Urmila had ten days before her passport expired, and four calls she had dodged for a month: the passport office, the electricity board about a wrong bill, the bank, and the municipal office about her address proof. The drilling from the flat upstairs made every call feel even worse.
Her friend Ira suggested a rule. "One call a day. Easiest first. Five minutes, then you're done."
On Monday Urmila called the electricity board. Her heart hammered, but the clerk just said, "Okay, madam, I'll correct it." Three minutes. On Tuesday the bank, slightly harder, but fine. By Thursday she dialled the passport office from the stairwell, away from the drilling, and got an appointment. She ticked it off and laughed. "That was it? I lost a month to that?"

qa.q: Which office did Urmila call first?
qa.a: The electricity board.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling before the first call?
qa.a: Her heart was hammering with fear and dread built up over a month of avoiding the calls.

qa.q: Why did Ira's one-call-a-day rule help?
qa.a: Starting with the easiest and keeping each call short showed the calls were bearable, so the dread shrank step by step until the passport call felt possible.

qa.q: How might Ira see Urmila's laugh at the end?
qa.a: Ira would probably feel pleased and relieved 🎉 that the small steps worked and Urmila could see the fear had been bigger than the calls.

grounding: An adult who avoids calls to offices makes one short call a day, easiest first, and the dread shrinks.

passage:
The rain had knocked out the power in the colony, so on the first evening of the Pongal holidays Jagdish showed his spelling test to his older brother Siddharth by candlelight. Nineteen words were ticked. One, "necessary", had a red circle.
"It's a disaster," Jagdish said, throwing the paper on the floor. "I'm stupid. I can't spell anything."
Siddharth picked it up and held it near the candle. "Nineteen out of twenty."
"But I got one WRONG. Everyone else probably got them all."
"Jagdish, count the ticks."
Jagdish refused and pulled his blanket over his head. From underneath came a muffled voice: "If it's not all right, it's all wrong."

qa.q: Which word did Jagdish spell wrong?
qa.a: "Necessary".

qa.q: Why did Jagdish call the test a disaster?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and frustrated; to him anything short of perfect counted as total failure, so one mistake made him feel stupid.

qa.q: What could Siddharth try next?
qa.a: Later, count the ticks together and treat the one word as something to practise, showing that nineteen right and one to learn is not failing.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the test?
qa.a: He sees nineteen out of twenty as a good result and stays patient, puzzled by how strongly Jagdish reacts.

grounding: A child who misspelled one word calls the whole test a disaster and himself stupid.

subtype: Skipping practice after a bad day [Actor]
passage:
So yeah, Shalini, I quit the running thing. You know I'd done it every morning since Diwali. Twenty-three mornings, all marked on the calendar with green ticks. Then last Tuesday it was so foggy and cold, and I stayed under the quilt. One day.
And when I saw that blank square, I was like, that's it. Streak's broken, plan's broken. What's the point of doing it half-perfect? Mummy said, "Just go tomorrow, Tushar." But it felt fake, starting again with a hole in it. So I haven't gone since. Nine days now.
Honestly, I kind of miss it. The quiet road, the tea-stall man waving. But it's either every day or nothing, right? Right?

qa.q: How many mornings had Tushar run before missing one?
qa.a: Twenty-three mornings.

qa.q: Why did Tushar stop running after one missed morning?
qa.a: Tushar felt disappointed and deflated by the broken streak, and with only two boxes, perfect or pointless, one blank square made the whole plan feel worthless.

qa.q: What could Tushar try instead?
qa.a: Count twenty-three out of twenty-four as a success, restart tomorrow with a simple rule like never missing two days in a row 👍, and let one gap stay just a gap.

qa.q: How might Shalini respond to the final "Right?"
qa.a: Shalini may sense that Tushar misses running and is half-asking to be talked out of quitting, so Shalini might gently disagree.

grounding: A teenager who missed one morning run decides the whole plan is over, seeing only perfect or pointless.

passage:
During the worst week of the May heat in Delhi, the flat's cooler leaked all over the floor. Tanvir came home, stepped in the puddle and exploded. "You never help with anything, Akash! You always mess everything up!"
Akash, who had cleaned the bathroom that very morning, felt his face go hot. "Never? I did the bathroom today. I fixed your fan last week!"
"That's not the point."
"You said never. That's literally the point."
They argued for fifteen minutes about "never" and "always", and nobody touched the puddle. Later, lying awake in the heat, Akash realised he still didn't know what Tanvir actually wanted him to do about the cooler.

qa.q: What had Akash cleaned that morning?
qa.a: The bathroom.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Tanvir said "You never help"?
qa.a: Akash felt hurt and defensive, unfairly painted after cleaning the bathroom that morning, so he fought the word "never".

qa.q: How could either of them get back to the real problem?
qa.a: Tanvir could name the specific issue, the leaking cooler and the puddle, and Akash could ask what was needed right now instead of arguing about the absolutes.

qa.q: What might have been going on for Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir was likely hot, tired and frustrated after stepping in the puddle, and the absolutes came out of that moment rather than a careful judgement.

grounding: A student told by his flatmate that he never helps feels unfairly painted, and they argue about the words instead of the leak.
